title: Undo a bad commit on a shared branch

scenario.brief:
**The incident.** A commit on `main` — *"perf: inline tax calc"* — accidentally removed the rounding from the tax calculation, so invoices show amounts like `7.4999999`. CI went red and caught it. It needs to be undone, now.

**The careful way.** `main` is shared — other people have already pulled it. So you must **not** rewrite history (that would break everyone else's copy). Instead you make a **new** commit that is the exact opposite of the bad one. That's what `git revert` does: it keeps the bad commit in the record, and adds an "undo" commit on top.

**Your step.**

- Revert the bad commit: `git revert <the bad commit>`. Git creates a new commit that puts the rounding back. (Its id is in the graph on the right, or `git log --oneline`.)

That's the whole fix. History stays honest — anyone can see both the mistake and the undo.
scenario.whyItMatters: On a shared branch you never rewrite what others have pulled. Revert is the safe undo: it fixes the problem by moving forward, not by erasing the past, so nobody else's repository breaks.

objectives.title: Add a revert commit that undoes the bad change
objectives.description: The newest commit should be a "Revert" of the bad one.
hints: `git revert` makes a new commit that is the opposite of the one you name.
Find the bad commit's id with `git log --oneline` (look for "inline tax calc"), then revert it.

objectives.title: The tax rounding is back, with history intact
objectives.description: Math.round is restored, and the bad commit is still in history (reverted, not erased).
hints: Reverting the bad commit restores the rounding line it removed — and keeps the bad commit in history.
Open `src/tax.js` (Math.round back), and `git log --oneline` should still show the bad commit under the revert.
If the bad commit is gone, you rewrote history (e.g. reset) instead of reverting. Undo and use `git revert`.

debrief.summary: You undid a bad commit on a shared branch the safe way — with a new revert commit — leaving history intact so nobody else's copy breaks.
internals: `git revert <id>` computed the reverse of that commit's change (what it added, remove; what it removed, add back) and committed that as a new commit.
The bad commit stays in history; the revert sits on top of it. `git log` shows both.
Nothing was rewritten, so anyone who already pulled main stays in sync — they just pull one more commit.
Compare with reset: reset moves the branch pointer and rewrites history, which is only safe on a branch no one else has.

keyCommands.note: Make a new commit that undoes commit <id>.
Use the default revert message without opening an editor.
See the bad commit and the revert together.

commonMistakes: Using reset --hard on a shared branch to 'remove' the bad commit, breaking everyone who already pulled it.
Thinking revert deletes the mistake — it records an undo instead.
debrief.atWork: When CI or a customer catches a bad change on main, revert is the standard, blameless fix: forward-only, safe for everyone, and easy to read in history later.
debrief.interview: "Difference between git revert and git reset?" Answer: revert adds a new commit that undoes a change and keeps history (safe on shared branches); reset moves the branch pointer and rewrites history (only safe locally).
